theory.intro: A **representative** sample reflects important features of its target population. Check who is included, who is left out, who chooses to respond and whether the sample may miss the population's variety.
facts: **Selection bias** occurs when the selected group does not fairly represent the population.
An incomplete selection list leaves out part of the target population. Random selection from that list cannot include the missing people.
**Volunteer bias** may occur when people choose whether to respond. Those who reply may have different views from those who do not.
A very **small sample** may miss the variety in the population.
**Survivorship bias** occurs when a sample includes successful cases but leaves out failures.
A large number of responses does not remove a problem with who is included or left out.

workedExamples.question_text: A council wants to know how residents travel to work. It interviews $180$ people at a bus stop on Tuesday morning. Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Only people at this bus stop at that time can be included.
Residents who drive, walk, cycle or work from home are missed.
Bus users are over-represented, so the sample may not reflect how all residents travel to work.

workedExamples.question_text: A council wants residents' opinions about a new road. It asks $4$ residents from a community of $720$. Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Four residents may miss much of the variety of opinions in the community.
The sample is too small to provide a strong basis for describing the whole community's views.

workedExamples.question_text: A website receives $650$ voluntary responses to a survey about whether people enjoy completing surveys. Almost all respondents say yes. Explain why it cannot conclude that almost everyone enjoys surveys.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The sample includes only people who choose to complete the survey.
People who dislike surveys may be less likely to respond.
The respondents may not represent the whole population, so their answers do not justify the conclusion.

workedExamples.question_text: A researcher investigates whether new businesses usually succeed by interviewing the owners of $75$ businesses that are still operating. Explain why the sample may be unrepresentative, with reference to survivorship bias.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The sample includes businesses that survived and are still operating.
Businesses that closed are left out.
This is survivorship bias: excluding failed businesses may make success appear more common than it is among all new businesses.

workedExamples.question_text: Engineers inspect $120$ aircraft that returned from missions. They observe many hits on the wings and body but very few around the cockpit. A statistician suggests placing extra armour around the cockpit. Explain why, with reference to survivorship bias.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The sample includes only aircraft that survived and returned.
Aircraft that did not return are left out, so this is survivorship bias.
Hits around the cockpit may have prevented aircraft from returning.
Few observed hits around the cockpit do not show that this area is safe.
Extra armour there may protect against damage that prevents survival, while the observed wing and body damage was survived by the returning aircraft.

foundation.question_text:
A researcher investigates the average weekly exercise hours of all adults in a town by surveying people exiting a gymnasium on Saturday morning.
Decide whether the sample is representative and name the over-represented group.
foundation.solution_text:
Gym users are over-represented, while adults who do not attend this gym at that time cannot be selected. Exercise habits of gym users may differ from those of other adults.
The selection does not fairly represent all adults in the town.

foundation.question_text:
A radio host asks listeners to text in whether they support higher tolls on the harbour bridge.
$1500$ listeners text in.
Decide whether the sample is representative and justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
Only listeners who choose to text are included. Their views may differ from other listeners and from people who do not listen to the station.
The 1500 replies do not remove self-selection or the restricted coverage.

foundation.question_text:
To estimate the proportion of voters in a state of $4\,000\,000$ people who support a new policy, a pollster randomly selects $5$ voters.
Decide whether this sample is representative and justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
Five randomly chosen voters may miss much of the variety of opinions among the state's voters.
This is a weak basis for representing the state's voters, even though selection is random.

foundation.question_text:
A high school wants to know whether students like a proposed change to the uniform. It surveys only $35$ students in Year 7.
Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative of the whole school.
foundation.solution_text:
Students in other year levels are left out.
Year 7 students may have different views and less experience of the previous uniform.
Their responses may not represent the views of students throughout the school.

foundation.question_text:
A researcher wants to know university students' favourite music genres. The researcher interviews $60$ students attending a classical music concert.
Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative.
foundation.solution_text:
Students attending the concert are more likely to enjoy classical music than other students.
Students who do not attend are left out.
The sample may over-represent a preference for classical music.

foundation.question_text:
A survey aims to determine the reading habits of all residents in a city by interviewing people at the central city library on a weekday afternoon.
Identify which subgroup is under-represented.
foundation.solution_text:
Residents who do not use the library at that time cannot be selected. This may under-represent people at work or school then and people who rarely use the library.
Their reading habits may differ, so this location and time do not fairly cover all residents.

foundation.question_text:
A researcher wants to know whether new shops in a town usually succeed. The researcher interviews owners of $45$ shops that are still open, leaving out shops that have closed.
Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative.
foundation.solution_text:
Only shops that survived and stayed open are included.
Shops that failed and closed are left out.
This is survivorship bias and may make success appear more common than it is among all new shops.

development.question_text:
A political polling organisation wants to survey voting intentions in an upcoming federal election.
They conduct phone interviews using landline numbers listed in the White Pages.
Explain why this sampling frame produces an unrepresentative sample.
development.solution_text:
The landline directory leaves out voters without listed landlines, including mobile-only households. Their views may differ from those of listed landline users.
Random selection within the directory cannot include the missing voters.

development.question_text:
A researcher wants to estimate weekly household spending across Australia. The researcher randomly selects $240$ households, all from one wealthy coastal suburb.
Explain why random selection does not make this sample representative of Australian households.
development.solution_text:
Random selection is limited to households in the wealthy suburb.
Households elsewhere cannot be selected, and their incomes and spending may differ.
The sample may overestimate typical household spending and does not fairly cover Australian households.

development.question_text:
An online shopping platform emails a customer satisfaction survey to all $50\,000$ customers who made a purchase last month.
$800$ customers complete the survey.
The company claims the sample represents all customers because every customer received the email.
Evaluate this claim.
development.solution_text:
Inviting everyone does not mean everyone is included in the responses. Only 800 of the 50,000 invited customers chose to answer; their experiences may differ from those who did not reply.
The invitation list alone does not establish that the responses represent all customers.

development.question_text:
A researcher interviews the owners of $300$ businesses that are still operating five years after opening. Most owners describe their businesses as successful.
The researcher concludes that most businesses succeed during their first five years. Explain why this conclusion is not justified.
development.solution_text:
The sample includes only businesses that remained open for five years.
Businesses that closed during that period are excluded.
This is survivorship bias, so the responses cannot establish how common success is among all businesses that opened.

development.question_text:
A dental clinic wants to know how satisfied local residents are with local healthcare.
The clinic distributes questionnaires to patients sitting in its waiting room.
Identify the selection mechanism causing bias and state the effect on the survey conclusion.
development.solution_text:
Only people attending this dental clinic at that time can be selected. Residents who use other services or cannot access this clinic are missed.
The patients' views may differ from those of other residents, so the sample does not fairly cover the local population. The information given does not show whether satisfaction would be overestimated or underestimated.

development.question_text:
A factory produces $500\,000$ microchips daily.
Quality control tests $10$ microchips chosen at random across the day and finds $0$ defects, concluding the entire daily batch has a $0\%$ defect rate.
Explain why this conclusion is unjustified.
development.solution_text:
Ten chips may miss the variety in the daily batch, including defective chips.
Finding no defects in the ten tested chips does not show that every untested chip is free of defects.
The small sample does not justify claiming a $0\%$ defect rate for the whole batch.

development.question_text:
A study investigates whether a training programme helps people find work. It interviews $90$ former participants who found jobs but leaves out participants who are still unemployed.
Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative, with reference to survivorship bias.
development.solution_text:
The sample includes only participants with the successful outcome of finding work.
Participants who did not find work are left out.
This is survivorship bias and may make the programme appear more successful than the experiences of all participants support.

mastery.question_text:
A social media influencer with $1\,000\,000$ followers runs a poll on their profile asking: 'Do you believe university degrees are worth the tuition cost?' $120\,000$ followers vote, with $85\%$ voting 'No'.
The influencer asserts that $85\%$ of young Australians reject university degrees.
Justify why this massive sample remains unrepresentative of young Australians.
mastery.solution_text:
1. Followers of this influencer do not cover all young Australians; their views and experiences may differ.
2. Only followers who choose to vote are included, so volunteer bias is possible.
3. More replies do not remove either of these selection problems. The 85% describes the 120,000 respondents, not necessarily all young Australians.

mastery.question_text:
During a conflict, engineers inspect $140$ aircraft that returned from missions. They find many hits on the wings but few on the engines. An engineer suggests adding armour around the engines rather than only where the returning aircraft show the most hits.
Explain this suggestion with reference to survivorship bias.
mastery.solution_text:
The inspected aircraft are only those that survived and returned.
Aircraft that did not return are missing from the sample.
Hits on engines may have prevented aircraft from returning, so few engine hits on surviving aircraft do not show that engines are safe.
The suggestion is to protect areas where damage may prevent survival, rather than relying only on damage observed on surviving aircraft.

mastery.question_text:
A researcher receives $2400$ voluntary replies to a survey asking whether people enjoy answering questionnaires. Of those who reply, $96\%$ say yes.
The researcher concludes that almost everyone in the community enjoys questionnaires. Explain why the conclusion is not valid despite the large number of replies.
mastery.solution_text:
People who enjoy questionnaires may be more willing to complete this survey.
People who dislike questionnaires may choose not to respond and are then left out.
The $96\%$ describes the respondents, whose views may differ from those of the whole community.
A large number of voluntary replies does not remove this selection problem.
